items.title: What You Will Pay for Medicare in 2027
items.summary:
Medicare premiums and deductibles are rising again in 2027 , making it critical for retirees to review their out-of-pocket costs during open enrollment. While Part A remains premium-free for most beneficiaries , costs for Part B outpatient care, Medicare Advantage plans, and standalone Part D drug coverage will all adjust in the coming year.

Medicare premiums and deductibles are due to increase in 2027 from 2026 levels , with Part B premiums rising by 3.2%. The Part A deductible increased by a smaller amount, 2.3%.

In addition to regular premiums, higher-income beneficiaries may owe an extra monthly surcharge on their Medicare Part B and Part D coverage, known as the income-related monthly adjustment amount ( IRMAA ). In 2027, high earners will pay an extra Part B surcharge of $83.70 to $502.40 on top of the standard Part B premium, plus a monthly Part D surcharge of $15.40 to $96.40. 

Individuals paying the smallest surcharges will owe $3,702 ($7,404 for couples) annually for Part B premiums and Part B and Part D surcharges. Total annual costs at the highest end will be $9,698.40 for individuals and $19,396.80 for couples. 

Whether you rely on original Medicare paired with a Medigap policy or choose a Medicare Advantage (MA) plan, understanding these baseline figures will help you anticipate healthcare expenses and protect your retirement cash flow in 2027.

(Image credit: Getty Images) Part A deductible and coinsurance Most Medicare beneficiaries don't pay a Part A monthly premium if they or their spouse paid Medicare taxes while working for at least 10 years (40…
items.t: What You Will Pay for Medicare in 2027

items.title: Why SNL’s Viral "Sister" Sketch Hit So Close to Home
items.summary:
A viral Saturday Night Live skit called "Sister" is making waves this week — not for taking on politics, but for exposing an uncomfortable truth about how families handle aging parents.

The parody pharma commercial opens with actor John Mulaney playing an earnest son who doesn't want to put his father in a nursing home, but can't afford a home health aide. "That's when I heard about Sister," he says. "Sister is a live-in 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free — and also your sister."

The mock commercial then pivots to the science behind the solution: "Years of internalized sexism warp Sister's brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility."

A scenario that's all too close to reality The skit drew millions of views because the data behind it isn't funny at all. The National Alliance for Caregiving and AARP say 63 million Americans are providing care today. But 61% of those caregivers are women, compared to 38% of men. 

The report also found that 64% of caregivers experience high emotional stress. Caregivers who feel forced into the role (56% of respondents) have worse mental health outcomes.

The financial toll on caregivers is also real. AARP reports that caregivers could lose $120,500, on average, over their lifetimes due to lost wages and future Social Security benefits. And the Center for the Study of Social Policy says female caregivers 50 and older have 58% less retirement wealth than those who aren't caregivers.

Rob Klein, long-term care planning strategist at CAREfidence , wasn't thrilled with the skit.

"While it got some laughs, it's actually…
items.t: Why SNL’s Viral "Sister" Sketch Hit So Close to Home

items.title: How to Avoid a Mutual Fund Tax Hit at Year-End
items.summary:
Investors are no doubt starting to think about their 2026 taxes, but the company that manages your mutual funds has been focused on the topic for a while. 

As fiscal years wrap up, typically at the end of October, fund companies start calculating how much of their funds’ income and capital gains they’ll distribute to investors before the end of the year. 

If you hold mutual funds in a tax-advantaged account, such as a 401(k) or an IRA, there’s not much to worry about. But if you own a mutual fund in your taxable brokerage account , you’ll owe taxes on that distribution, so it’s best to have a plan.

What often catches investors off guard is that the tax liability crops up even if they don’t buy or sell a fund share over the course of the year. Worse, it’s often the funds that have performed particularly badly during the year that pay outsized distributions. 

"If you’re seeing a big distribution in a down year, that’s just insult added to injury," says Holly Swan , head of wealth solutions at Allspring Global Investments.

It helps to be prepared by knowing more about whether your fund is planning a distribution — and if so, how much — as well as what you can do to minimize your tax bill.

Here’s how it works: When a mutual fund sells a stock, bond, or other investment it owns, it either makes a profit or takes a loss. At the end of the year, if gains outweigh the losses, funds are required to pass that amount to investors. 

The annual distribution also includes income from dividends or interest. Fund shareholders who hold their shares in a taxable account must then pay…
items.t: How to Avoid a Mutual Fund Tax Hit at Year-End

items.title: Dying Rich vs Living Well: Guide to Wise Retirement Spending
items.summary:
For most of our working lives, the financial instructions were pretty simple: 

Earn money Save money Invest money Don't buy something ridiculous because your neighbor bought one Then you retire , and suddenly, the rules change.

You're no longer primarily accumulating money. You're trying to make it last. You're navigating Social Security , Medicare, taxes, required minimum distributions ( RMDs ), inflation, adult children, grandchildren and a seemingly endless parade of people who would be delighted to separate you from your savings.

Welcome to the new economy for older people. And here's the problem: So many financial pundits spend decades teaching people how to save for retirement and remarkably little time teaching them how to manage money once they're actually retired. As a financial literacy expert, that is my focus for this article. 

Here are some rules to keep in mind for your transition from the accumulation phase to the spending phase of retirement.

Rule No. 1: Stop thinking of your nest egg as a pile of money A million dollars sounds like a fortune … until it has to pay you a salary for 25 or 30 years. That's the mental shift retirees need to make. Your IRA isn't a jackpot. It's your personal pension fund.

items.title: IRS Increases 2027 FSA Limits Just in Time for Open Enrollment
items.summary:
With many household budgets stretched thin and medical costs continuing to climb, finding ways to make every paycheck stretch a little further matters more than ever. 

Fortunately, the IRS recently announced new 2027 contribution limits for tax-advantaged healthcare accounts like health flexible spending accounts (FSAs).

With an FSA, employees can make payroll deposits to help pay insurance deductibles or other qualifying medical expenses (including items not covered by insurance). 

And if you participate in one of these accounts, your contributions are tax-free. That means they are generally not subject to federal income tax, Social Security taxes, or Medicare taxes .

However, you cannot exceed the annual contribution limit — your employer's payroll will typically cap your deductions, and any accidental excess (such as from switching jobs mid-year with a dependent care FSA) will be taxed at ordinary federal income tax rates .

But with FSA contributions higher for 2027 than last year, there's much more to know this open enrollment season. Read on.

FSA limits 2027 Flexible spending accounts use your contributions to pay certain out-of-pocket health care costs for yourself, your spouse, and your dependents. As mentioned, the money you chip into the account is tax-free.

If you have an FSA account, here are the maximum amounts you can contribute for 2027 (tax returns normally filed in 2028).

The FSA contribution limit for 2027 is $3,500; that’s up from $3,400 the previous year. If your spouse has a plan through their employer, they may also contribute up to $3,500…
items.t: IRS Increases 2027 FSA Limits Just in Time for Open Enrollment

items.title: Are You Spending Too Little in Retirement? Ask Yourself These 3 Questions
items.summary:
Are you skipping that week-long Mediterranean cruise because gas prices are too high? Passing on dinner out because grocery bills keep climbing? Or holding back because you fear your money won't last thirty years of retirement? 

If so, you're in good company. Millions of retirees are sitting on hard-earned nest eggs, fearing their savings will run dry.

For many, that fear is unfounded. According to research from the Employee Benefit Research Institute, most retirees still have roughly 60% to 70% of their savings left untouched even after two decades in retirement. 

Even if you are legacy-minded and hope to leave an inheritance to your kids, you may have extra money you can spend. Sometimes, permitting yourself to use it comes down to a little soul-searching and smart financial planning.

Are you spending enough in retirement? Ask yourself these 3 questions:

1. Do I have enough reliable income to cover my expenses? 

(Image credit: Getty Images) Peace of mind is essential in retirement. That's why financial advisers say the first question to ask yourself is simple: Are your basic monthly bills covered? If the answer is yes, you can start opening the purse strings with much more confidence.

"To what degree are the essentials covered with income you can rely on?" says Joseph Sicchitano , head of individual solutions at Principal Financial Group.

Reliable income usually means Social Security , a pension, savings, or some combination of the three. "If your plan can support $6,000 a month and you are getting by nicely on $5,000, then you can probably spend a little bit…
items.t: Are You Spending Too Little in Retirement? Ask Yourself These 3 Questions

items.title: Does Your Car Insurance Cover These 5 Cold-Weather Problems?
items.summary:
Winter is full of hazards for your vehicle. You might wake up after a snowstorm to find a tree branch has fallen on your car. Or you might hit black ice during your commute and slide into a guardrail. 

These situations can cause thousands of dollars in damage, and you might expect your car insurance to cover the expense. But whether your insurer will pay depends on the type of coverage you carry.

Before freezing temperatures and snowy roads become part of your daily routine, take some time to review your policy. Here's a look at five common winter hazards, what your car insurance may cover and where you might have gaps in coverage.

Understand what your car insurance covers before winter weather hits Before winter weather arrives, take a look at your current coverage. Insurers offer three main types of car insurance : 

Liability insurance: Generally required by states, liability coverage pays for injuries and property damage you cause to others in an accident. It doesn't cover damage to your own vehicle. Collision insurance: Collision coverage helps pay to repair or replace your vehicle if you hit another car or object. That may include accidents caused by icy or snowy roads, regardless of whether you're at fault. A deductible typically applies. Comprehensive insurance: Comprehensive insurance covers damage to your vehicle from non-collision events, such as falling branches, hail, theft and certain types of windshield damage. A deductible typically applies. Most states require drivers to carry a minimum amount of liability insurance , but comprehensive and collision…
items.t: Does Your Car Insurance Cover These 5 Cold-Weather Problems?

Toss in a lame-duck President Donald Trump representing Republicans for the final two years of his second term, and you've got a potent recipe for political gridlock.

Before the election, I pointed readers toward Dan Burrows' warning about positioning one's portfolio based on the expected outcome of electoral politics:

I think that sentiment also applies to any predictions one might make based on actual election results … especially when those results point to a high likelihood of one political party sending bill after bill into the other party's veto chipper.

On the other hand, we can't exactly ignore Washington's power struggle and what the…

items.title: How Today's Annuities Can Boost Your Retirement Readiness
items.summary:
Three years of strong market returns can make someone planning for retirement feel like the goal is within reach. 

However, a growing account balance doesn't automatically translate into a stream of reliable income that will be needed to cover decades of living expenses.

A recent BlackRock study found that 68% of 60-plus-year-olds believe they are on track for retirement. Yet their workplace retirement savings are projected to generate only 50% to 60% of the income they expected to need — a consequential gap for a retirement that could last 30 years or more.

So, what is the best way forward? The standard advice is to save more, but mortgages, student loans, childcare costs, aging parents and other real-life demands can make that difficult. 

Fortunately, saving more is not the only path to having more retirement income when you need it. Another option is to create a personal pension: A stream of income you can't outlive, funded by a modern, low-cost annuity.

Prepare to fund more of retirement on your own For decades, Americans drew retirement income from three sources: An employer pension , Social Security and personal savings. That structure hasn't disappeared, but the weight each source carries has shifted — and more of it now falls on you.

Employer pension plans. These once provided steady lifetime income for generations of Americans. Today, traditional pension plans are rare. 

Instead, companies offer 401(k)s and similar workplace plans that shift the primary responsibility for turning accumulated assets into retirement income for individuals.

items.t: How Today's Annuities Can Boost Your Retirement Readiness

items.title: Using a Walker Isn’t Surrendering to Old Age
items.summary:
Persuading an aging parent to accept help — especially when it comes to mobility assistance — can be a daunting challenge for any family. 

Many older people, such as Dan, a faithful reader and father, fear that using a four-wheel walker, or rollator, signals a final surrender to old age, and they choose instead to risk dangerous falls rather than compromise their independence or self-image. 

Here's the email I received from his daughter and son: 

"Our 80-year-old father, Dan, refuses to use a rollator, saying, 'I don't want to look old, and besides, these things are too heavy for me to put in the trunk of my car.' He has horrible balance problems, uses a cane poorly and has fallen several times.

"We found your story about a 40-year-old carpenter who made measurement errors due to poor eyesight and was at risk of losing his job, but he refused to get glasses because he didn't want to look old. You persuaded him to see an eye doctor , and he got glasses, saving his job. 

"Dad loves your column, so we need your help. Will you please talk with him? Thanks, Serena and Jimmy."

Sadly, this is a common reason to avoid using a walker When I heard "because I don't want to look old," at first I couldn't believe it, thinking, "For God's sake, man, you are 80. What's more important — risking a bad fall or looking old?" Then I wondered whether that is a common excuse for others not using a walker/rollator.

items.title: Here's What Berkshire Hathaway Bought and Sold in Q3
items.summary:
After overseeing a major housecleaning of Berkshire Hathaway's ( BRK.B ) equity portfolio to start his tenure as CEO, Greg Abel continued with a sizable shift in capital deployment during the third quarter (Q3) of 2026.

Berkshire was once again a net seller of equities in the third quarter, to the tune of $426 million. With the exception of Q2, the holding company has sold more stock than it bought for 14 of the past 15 quarters.

That said, Berkshire did up its exposure to equities enough in the previous quarter that it remained a net buyer of stocks for the first nine months of 2026. For the year to date, the conglomerate purchased a net of more than $11 billion in equities. 

At the same time, Abel continued to buy back Berkshire Hathaway stock, something his predecessor Warren Buffett was more reluctant to do. The company repurchased $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock in Q3, bringing its full-year stock buybacks to more than $14 billion.

Abel oversees Berkshire's equity portfolio , although Buffett, who stepped down as chairman in September, remains available in an advisory role. Be that as it may, this is Abel's show. And as in the second quarter, the company revealed no flashy new positions or big additions in a Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing on November 16. Indeed, Abel continued most of the trends we saw three months ago.

Berkshire further boosted stakes in some existing positions, and it also continued to pare back on some legacy holdings. Interestingly, Berkshire cut back on some investments in the financial sector, including long-time…

You'll get all the latest news first by subscribing, but we will publish many (but not all) of the forecasts a few days afterward online. Here’s the latest… 

As the dust settles on the midterm elections, Congress returns its attention to legislating. The GOP is left with only a few more weeks in charge before handing control over to the Democrats in January. The Republicans’ to-do list for this “lame-duck” period is evolving, but they won’t have time for everything. 

Priority number one is securing government funding, which expires December 11, to avoid a shutdown . Republicans are eager to act while they’re in power, but Democrats will demand concessions, like action on the Iran war. As a result, the odds of a shutdown have increased, although a deal remains possible. 

Second is an annual defense policy bill, the must-pass National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which also sets the Pentagon’s budget for the year. Congress normally passes the NDAA without fail. It will likely do so again this year, though negotiations will be messy and require compromises by both parties. The biggest sticking point: Iran war funding, which could derail either of the must-pass bills. Dems will push for a provision to cut off the money. items.title: Here's How to Prepare for a Bank Outage
items.summary:
The Associated Press reports that customers of Chase, U.S. Bank, and Wells Fargo have experienced service disruptions. Customers began encountering issues this morning, with more customers being impacted by early afternoon. 

A Chase spokesperson informed the AP that technical issues caused some transactions to take longer than usual, but customers have access to their accounts and money. Meanwhile, CBS News reported that Truist and Capital One customers also faced difficulties accessing their online accounts.

Coming on the heels of major outages with Microsoft Outlook and Teams, as well as the FAA grounding flights for hours on Friday, tech has had a challenging week. 

Outages can occur unexpectedly and typically last only a few hours. However, being unable to access your funds when needed highlights the importance of preparing for bank outages in advance. Here are several proactive steps you can take.

What to do if your bank is down right now If you're experiencing a bank outage, check your bank's official website or social media channels for service updates. You may still be able to access your money by visiting a local branch or using an ATM.

Avoid repeatedly submitting payments or transfers, as this could result in duplicate transactions once services are restored. Keep a record of any failed transactions and fees incurred during the outage so you can follow up with your bank.

Finally, be on the lookout for scammers posing as bank representatives. Never share your login credentials or security codes with someone who contacts you claiming they can restore access…
items.t: When Tech Fails Your Bank: What to Do When Chase Goes Offline

items.title: A Year-End Review Can Align Your Investments, Taxes, Goals
items.summary:
At year-end, many investors review gains and look for ways to manage their tax bills. A more meaningful review also asks whether their investment strategy, account structure, charitable goals and future priorities remain aligned.

The goal isn't simply to reduce this year's taxes . It's to improve after-tax outcomes over time without losing sight of risk, liquidity, costs and long-term objectives.

That's why the most impactful financial planning strategies include tight coordination between bankers, financial advisers and tax professionals.

Start with after-tax returns Taxes matter, but they shouldn't dictate investment decisions. A tax-saving investment isn't necessarily a good investment, and avoiding a taxable gain shouldn't prevent a change that supports long-term goals.

Depending on an investor's goals, municipal bonds , exchange-traded funds (ETFs) , separately managed accounts that hold individual securities and other tax-managed strategies might help improve tax efficiency while supporting the portfolio's overall direction.

A more useful year-end question: Is my portfolio still positioned to meet my goals after taxes, fees and investment risk?

items.title: We Have Generous Pensions. Do We Still Need Retirement Savings?
items.summary:
Dear Wealth Wise: My husband and I are both teachers in our late 40s. We're eligible to retire in our mid-to-late 50s and collect a full pension of a little more than 50% of our salaries, plus state-paid health benefits. We're also eligible for Social Security in our 60s. We haven't saved for retirement, given all this. We want to stop teaching as soon as we can get our full pensions and work part-time somewhere for a few years until we turn 65. Is this a good plan, or should we start contributing to our 403(b)s? 

While many private-sector workers would love the stability of pensions, they're a rarity these days. Only 14% of private-sector workers have access to a traditional defined benefit plan, according to a March 2026 Bureau of Labor Statistics report . 

By contrast, 86% of state and local government workers have access to a pension . That can take some of the pressure off retirement planning. 

Here, we have a couple who work as teachers and are eligible for a generous pension. They haven't specified the estimated monthly benefit they expect, but the median state and local government pension was $2,078 in 2024, the most recent data available. That would leave them with over $4,100 a month in today's dollars — an enviable amount of guaranteed income. 

Will the promise of steady income for life let them off the hook when it comes to retirement savings ? Not so fast, our experts say. 

A pension is a foundation, not a substitute for retirement savings The guaranteed income a pension provides can make retirement seem less scary. But that doesn't mean workers with…
items.t: We Have Generous Pensions. Do We Still Need Retirement Savings?

items.title: Why You Need Estate Planning Before You Feel Wealthy
items.summary:
Estate planning is often associated with families that have substantial fortunes, complicated trusts or an obvious tax issue. In practice, the need for deliberate estate planning can arise in families whose circumstances may appear far less complex at first glance.

A household can spend decades saving consistently, building retirement balances and watching a home appreciate without ever thinking of itself as particularly wealthy. Yet the financial picture may now include several types of assets, different beneficiary arrangements, a surviving spouse who will need flexibility, and children with different circumstances. 

The consequences of how those pieces fit together have become more significant, even if everyday life has changed very little.

The useful threshold is therefore not a particular net worth . It is the point at which ownership, liquidity and transfer decisions have become important enough that leaving them to default rules could produce an outcome the family didn't intend.

When your financial life becomes more complex than it feels Two households with similar net worth can have very different estate planning needs because the composition and purpose of their assets may be entirely different.

One family may hold most of its assets in liquid investments. Another may have substantial value concentrated in a home, real estate or a privately held business. 

One couple may expect to use most of what it has accumulated during retirement, while another places a high priority on leaving a legacy to children or grandchildren.

items.title: 5 Key Principles That Help You Build Financial Confidence
items.summary:
In my 42 years in financial services, one lesson has stood the test of time: Markets change, investment strategies come and go, and headlines shift daily, but human behavior around money remains remarkably consistent.

There is always a "next big thing" competing for attention, from dot-com stocks to cryptocurrencies to artificial intelligence. Through the noise, people want financial control, but many feel uncertain about whether they're making the right choices .

According to a new Financial Confidence report from Edelman Financial Engines (EFE), 84% of Americans prefer to stay actively engaged in retirement and savings decisions, yet only 40% of them know exactly how their 401(k) is invested. 

This disconnect between people's desire to take control of their financial future and their confidence in the decisions they're making is what EFE calls the Financial Confidence Gap.

This captures much of what I've seen throughout my career. People aren't looking for the next hot stock — they want reassurance they're making sound financial decisions. Helping people navigate uncertainty, whether that was Black Monday, the 2008 financial crisis or the pandemic, has defined the past four decades of my work.

Financial confidence doesn't come from guessing what the markets will do next. It comes from being prepared for whatever they do and knowing when to seek financial advice.

items.title: Is Selling the Family Heirloom Socially Acceptable?
items.summary:
Losing someone you care about brings profound sorrow, and when they leave you something valuable, the gift can make you feel conflicted. 

On one hand, you're thankful because it serves as a reminder of the fond memories you have of that loved one. On the other, what if you don't need what they left, and you could really benefit from selling it? 

This is a situation many people find themselves in and are unsure how to handle. Here's when it's socially acceptable to sell a family heirloom. 

When should I sell an heirloom? 

(Image credit: Getty Images) Richard Tilles , president of CIRCA, told Kiplinger that he sees people struggling with this all the time, and his advice is to keep it if it holds value or use it for yourself. It's going to be worth more to you than to potential buyers. 

However, he advises that if you don't have specific plans for the heirloom and it will sit around or get lost, sell it. 

When looking for a place to sell the heirloom, Tilles recommends taking it for an estimate from three different buyers. Look for those with an established reputation. Doing this can help you fetch a better price. 

Which items are fetching higher and lower values right now? 

(Image credit: Getty Images) Gold is at a historical price, Tilles says. Clients are shocked at how much gold jewelry is worth. People selling nice pieces from the 1970s and 1980s are getting almost twice as much today as they would have a few years ago.

Meanwhile, some items have dropped in value. Diamond pins from the 1950s have cooled down. They still have value, but less than they did 15…
items.t: Is Selling the Family Heirloom Socially Acceptable?
